edges.description: With surface regulation lost, C3b deposited on endothelium is no longer inactivated and the alternative-pathway amplification loop runs unchecked.
A convertase that forms more readily or resists inactivation produces the same unchecked amplification on endothelial surfaces as loss of regulation, reached from the opposite direction.

Sustained diacylglycerol/protein kinase C signalling in endothelium and platelets drives the same microvascular thrombosis that complement-driven endothelial injury produces, which is why the two genetic routes converge on one clinical syndrome.

nodes.description: The central mechanism of aHUS is loss of regulation of the alternative complement pathway on endothelial cell surfaces. Normally, complement factor H (CFH), membrane cofactor protein (MCP/CD46), and factor I (CFI) cooperate to inactivate C3b deposited on host cell surfaces. In aHUS, genetic mutations in these regulators or gain-of-function mutations in complement effectors (CFB, C3) lead to unchecked C3 convertase (C3bBb) activity and amplification loop activation on endothelial surfaces.

nodes.description: The one aHUS mechanism in this entry that is not complement-mediated. Diacylglycerol kinase epsilon phosphorylates arachidonic acid-containing diacylglycerol to phosphatidic acid, terminating a diacylglycerol signal that activates protein kinase C. Biallelic loss of DGKE therefore leaves that signal running in endothelium, platelets and podocytes, producing a prothrombotic state directly rather than through the alternative pathway.

nodes.description: Factor H, factor I and membrane cofactor protein together restrain the alternative pathway on host cell surfaces, and loss-of-function variants in any of them remove that restraint. In the CFH case the disease-associated variants cluster in the C-terminal surface-recognition domains, so plasma C3 regulation is preserved while regulation on renal endothelium fails. Homozygous deletion of CFHR1 and CFHR3 reaches the same endpoint acquired rather than inherited, by predisposing to anti-factor H autoantibodies that neutralise the regulator.
